item.title: The British island that made a deal with nature
item.description:

Why it is here: clear reporting, concrete detail

Lundy Island in the Bristol Channel, UK, showcases a pioneering conservation success with thriving wildlife, a fishing community, and a no-take marine zone. Rats were eradicated in the early 2000s, leading to a seabird population increase from 6,000 to 48,000. The UK's first marine nature reserve and no-take zone were established in 2003, benefiting species like puffins and lobsters. Local fishermen and conservationists collaborated to create the zone, leading to increased lobster populations and improved fishing conditions.

item.title: As Nepal celebrates the crow, urban sprawl and waste drive strain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Nepal celebrates Kaag Tihar, honoring crows as divine messengers. Urban sprawl in Kathmandu has expanded by 124% since 1989, reducing green space by 54%. Tree removal has forced crows to nest on utility poles, while waste attracts dense crow and kite populations. This has led to public health issues, including an H5N1 outbreak. Bird ecologist Hem Bahadur Katuwal argues crows are beneficial for waste cleanup, and the issue lies with poor waste management and habitat destruction. The Kathmandu Metropolitan City is working on bird conservation and tree preservation.
